Remember: parents offer advice, teachers teach knowledge, and counselors help students understand themselves. Once students gain that clarity, their path becomes easier to see.

A common path is: study education, psychology, or social work; earn a counseling or career-planning credential; gain case experience through an internship in a school counseling or career center; then begin as an assistant counselor and progress toward counselor, curriculum specialist, or counseling center supervisor.

This career suits patient people with empathy and broad knowledge. It can fit if you hear the anxiety a student has not voiced, explain employment data and academic options clearly, and mediate between parents and students.

Educational, Guidance, And Career Counselors And Advisors provide academic planning, subject and college application guidance, career counseling, and psychological support in schools and education organizations. They use assessments and counseling methods to help students understand themselves and make choices, while coordinating support from families and schools.

paragraphs: Daily work combines individual counseling, classes, and coordination. Counselors listen to students in counseling rooms, teach career topics in classrooms, and coordinate with teachers and parents in offices. Subject selection and college applications create peak workloads in high school. Postsecondary roles focus more on employment guidance and career planning, so the pace varies by education level.

AI can clearly list what each major leads to and how much it pays, but only a counselor in the room can hear what lies behind a student's fear whenever science subjects come up.

According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), about 376,300 counselors worked in education in 2024. Employment is projected to reach 389,600 by 2034, a net gain of about 13,300 jobs, with about 31,000 openings each year. Median annual pay was about $65,100 in 2026 (BLS OOH, 2026).

AI is narrowing the information gap in education and career planning. Students and parents can search major databases, career matches, salary data, and subject-selection advice themselves. Yet counseling is about self-understanding and choice. Determining what suits a student, what drives their anxiety, and how to reconcile family expectations with the student's wishes requires trust and professional judgment. AI provides data, but not direction or empathy.

paragraphs: A score of 5/10 places this occupation in the moderate AI exposure range. AI is taking over much of the information and matching work, but individual understanding, trust, and guidance through decisions remain central. AI can present the options, but it cannot know the person or accompany them through a decision. Jobs will shift from providing information to deeper counseling.

Moderate risk still means change. Counselors who only recite major lists and employment data face replacement by AI. Counselors who use data tools and understand psychology and communication become more valuable because they provide deeper service. Treat AI as the researcher and yourself as the counselor.

For a student considering this career, education or psychology is a useful major. Build experience in counseling and career development while in school. Parents should also keep planning in perspective: it is an aid, while the student's wishes and abilities remain central. Counseling should not become an outlet for parental anxiety.

Use assessments, data platforms, and AI matching while developing counseling skill and case experience. Progress toward a school counseling center, counseling supervisor role, or independent practice. Move from information provider to in-depth counselor.

People with teaching, human resources, or psychological counseling experience can make a relatively smooth transition. Start with a career-planning or counseling credential, then seek an assistant counselor role at a school or agency. Real cases and communication examples often matter more in interviews than certificates alone.

Do not reduce counselors to information clerks; AI handles that work. Give counselors data tools and manageable caseloads so they can focus on deeper counseling. Supervision and case reviews build professional skill and help retain strong counselors.

This career suits people who enjoy helping others gain clarity. Watching a confused student move from not knowing what to choose to knowing what they want provides a strong sense of purpose.

The value of this work lies in witnessing choices. A counselor helps a student struggling with subject selection understand what they want. Three years later, the student returns with an offer from their preferred university. Helping a confused student find direction creates a tangible sense of achievement.

If you enjoy helping people think through choices and can synthesize complex information, educational and career guidance offers professional depth and social value.

paragraphs: The greatest career risks are weak professional boundaries and burnout, not AI. AI replaces information delivery. Long-term success depends on managing parental expectations and maintaining sound professional boundaries.

The greatest risks come from pressure and the boundaries of advice, not AI. Students and parents hold high expectations, and counselors can be blamed for poor college application or career choices. Many jobs are in school systems with limited authorized positions and narrow promotion paths. The work can also carry a heavy emotional load.

School psychologists focus on identifying and addressing psychological problems. Educational counselors focus on academic planning, subject selection, further study, and career development. One addresses mental health concerns; the other helps chart a path.

AI will replace information-heavy tasks, but not in-depth counseling. AI can retrieve data and generate matches. Understanding a student, building trust, and reconciling family expectations with the student's wishes require an ongoing counseling relationship that AI cannot provide.

These abilities include understanding individuals beyond assessment results, building enough trust for students to speak honestly, reconciling parental expectations with a student's wishes, integrating data with personality and context, and providing continued guidance after a choice.

This career suits people with empathy, patience, strong information-synthesis skills, good communication and coordination, and sound professional boundaries. It does not suit forceful lecturers who lack patience or offer abstract advice without practical steps.

They work in counseling and career centers at secondary schools and universities, education consulting agencies, admissions-planning companies, and employment guidance departments at vocational institutions. Most work takes place on campuses or in agency offices.

Yes, but the work must become deeper. Earn a career-planning or counseling credential, build strong counseling skills and case experience, and use AI tools to reduce routine work. Counselors who can guide people through choices will remain in demand.
